newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.S. widow of Guatemala guerrilla dealt legal blow.
newsitem.headline: U.S. widow of Guatemala guerrilla dealt legal blow.

text.p: Guatemala's highest court on Friday refused to recognise a U.S. woman's marriage to a now dead guerrilla fighter, dealing a blow to her battle to sue army personnel suspected in his torture and death.
"The Constitutional Court declared the supposed marriage in Texas is not legal in Guatemala," Solicitor General Acisclo Valladares said in a statement.

U.S. lawyer Jennifer Harbury has fought for four years to uncover the truth about the 1992 disappearance and death of guerrilla commander Efrain Bamaca, whom she said she married in an informal ceremony in Texas in front of friends.
She has tried to get the marriage recognised officially in Guatemala so that she can be named as plaintiff in lawsuits against army personnel suspected in Bamaca's death.
Harbury staged hunger strikes in Guatemala City in 1994 and in front of the White House in 1995 to publicise her case.
Partly due to her pressure a special White House panel issued a report early this year regarding CIA knowledge of the deaths of Americans and relatives of Americans here.
That report said that Bamaca was tortured after he was seized by the army in March 1992 and that paid CIA informants in Guatemala knew about his torture and death.
Harbury's marriage was made official by a judge in Texas after Bamaca had disappeared. At the time, she did not know whether he was dead or alive.

A lower court here agreed to register the marriage. But Valladares petitioned the Constitutional Court to nullify that registration, arguing that marriages with only one party present are not legal in Guatemala.
The government and guerrillas plan to sign a definitive peace treaty in December, ending Central America's longest civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, many of them civilians.
